solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Town known for tick-borne disease admits average body full of enzymes

indicators.note: a town that admits something lets it inside, so one word goes within the other

parts.note: Lyme in Connecticut gave its name to Lyme disease, spread by ticks
so-so means middling, average

explanation.surface: A news item about a town famous for a tick-borne illness taking in some unremarkable body.
explanation.walkthrough: Lyme disease takes its name from the town of Lyme in Connecticut, USA.
explanation.definitionFit: A lysosome is a cell organelle packed with digestive enzymes, so it is literally a tiny body full of them.

clue.text: Pike's not compact according to commentator

indicators.note: a commentator speaks, so we want what is heard rather than what is written

parts.note: something not compact is loose

explanation.surface: A sports pundit remarks that a player called Pike is not keeping a tight formation.
explanation.walkthrough: The capital P dresses the fish up as a person's name; the 's is just 'is'.
explanation.definitionFit: Luce is an old word for the pike, the freshwater predatory fish, especially a full-grown one.

clue.text: Ordeal (standard scrape) in places for birds

indicators.note: the bracketed words sit in the word for places, enclosed by it

parts.note: to set is to place, so places is sets
an ordeal is a hellish experience: hell
par is the standard or norm
to rake is to scrape over a surface

explanation.surface: Someone describes a gruelling, routine scraping job carried out in aviaries.
explanation.walkthrough: The brackets in the clue neatly group the three pieces that go inside places.
explanation.definitionFit: Shell parrakeet is an old name for the budgerigar, the small Australian parrot with scalloped plumage, so these are birds.

clue.text: Swallowing drink quickly, was disgusting, all told in few words

indicators.note: told means spoken aloud, so the combined sounds are heard rather than spelt

parts.note: 'sucked' (was disgusting, slang) is said SUCKT; swallowing SINK (drink quickly, as in sink a pint) inside it gives SUCK-SINK-T

explanation.surface: Someone gulped a drink that tasted foul, and summed it up tersely.
explanation.walkthrough: 'sucked' is pronounced with a final T sound; put 'sink' inside it, between the K and T sounds, and 'all told' says the whole aloud, exactly like the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Succinct means briefly and clearly expressed, using few words.

clue.text: Longhairs say this without point being raised

indicators.note: in a down entry, raising something turns it upside down so it reads bottom to top

parts.note: w/o is the written abbreviation for without
to point a gun is to aim it

explanation.surface: Hippies talk about life without purpose being brought up.
explanation.walkthrough: Longhairs are long-haired cats, not hippies; WO AIM read upwards gives the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Miaow is the cry of a cat, so it is what long-haired breeds such as Persians utter.

clue.text: Toff in Sun means to manipulate text

indicators.note: one word placed in another sits inside it

parts.note: Sol is the Sun, from Latin
a nob is a toff, a posh person

explanation.surface: A posh figure in a tabloid newspaper is accused of twisting the story.
explanation.walkthrough: S(NOB)OL. The Sun is a British tabloid, which makes manipulating text a pointed phrase.
explanation.definitionFit: SNOBOL is an early programming language designed for processing and transforming strings of characters.

clue.text: Northerner's guffaw apparently appealing to a more specialised group

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a Scots and northern dialect word for a snigger or neigh-like laugh

definitions.text: appealing to a more specialised group
definitions.meaning: second meaning: read as a comparative of niche, a whimsical coinage

explanation.walkthrough: 'Apparently' admits the second reading is a jokey made-up comparative of niche.
explanation.definitionFit: In dialect it is a noun for a loud snorting laugh; split up it looks like 'more niche', targeting a narrower audience.

clue.text: Is last pub to host rounds on an equal high level?

indicators.note: a pub that hosts something has it inside the premises

parts.note: a bar is a pub
rings are circles, rounds
'up there' with the best means on an equally high level

explanation.surface: Someone asks whether the final pub of the evening will lay on drinks rounds of equally top quality.
explanation.walkthrough: B(RINGS UP THERE)AR: the bar hosts both pieces, and 'rounds' are rings rather than drinks.
explanation.definitionFit: To bring up the rear is an idiom for coming at the very back of a procession or field, finishing at the end.

clue.text: Ear parts, bristly, almost hang out

indicators.note: out means not in proper order, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: almost means not quite complete, so the last letter of hang is dropped

parts.note: only HAN is used once its last letter goes

explanation.surface: Hairy bits of the ear nearly stick out.
explanation.walkthrough: 'almost' cuts hang to HAN; 'out' then rearranges BRISTLY and HAN together.
explanation.definitionFit: The labyrinths are the inner ear's maze of canals, the bony and membranous parts of the ear.

clue.text: Room in unpleasant A&E providing prescriptions?

indicators.note: a word placed in another sits inside it

parts.note: foul means nasty, unpleasant
RM is the standard abbreviation for room
taken as written, minus the ampersand

explanation.surface: A grim hospital emergency department room where patients are handed their prescriptions.
explanation.walkthrough: FO(RM)UL then AE. A&E is the British name for a hospital emergency room.
explanation.definitionFit: Formulae are fixed recipes or prescribed methods; the question mark flags that prescriptions here means set procedures rather than medicines.

clue.text: Guy briefly entering nerve centre in Anchorage who's not been there long

indicators.note: entering means going inside, so the shortened guy word sits within the nerve word

parts.note: cheek means nerve, audacity

indicators.note: briefly means cut short, so the last letter of chap is lost

parts.note: a chap is a guy, a man

indicators.note: centre in picks the single middle letter of Anchorage

parts.note: a city in Alaska; its fifth of nine letters is O

explanation.surface: A man briefly enters a nerve centre in an Alaskan city.
explanation.walkthrough: 'nerve centre' looks like one phrase but splits: nerve is the first piece, and 'centre in' goes with Anchorage. 'Guy briefly' loses its last letter before 'entering'. Cheechako is Alaskan slang, so Anchorage also sets the scene.
explanation.definitionFit: Cheechako is the Alaskan and Yukon slang term for a newcomer or tenderfoot.

clue.text: Ape with extra loop at the stern channel for draining deck

indicators.text: with extra loop at the stern
indicators.note: adding a second loop at the bottom (stern) of the letter P turns it into the letter B

parts.note: a chimp is an ape
the letter P with a loop added below its bowl

explanation.surface: A monkey with an additional rope loop at a ship's back end, and a deck drain.
explanation.walkthrough: 'with extra loop at the stern' is visual: draw a second bowl at the foot of P and it becomes B. Stern keeps up the nautical surface while meaning the bottom of the letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Chimb, also spelt chime, is a channel cut in a waterway on a ship's deck to carry off water.

clue.text: See, primarily in East London, receding shallow lake there

parts.note: v is short for Latin vide, see

indicators.note: receding means moving back, so the letters run backwards
primarily points to the first letter of each following word

parts.note: first letters of in, East and London

explanation.surface: A tourist tip to go and see a shallow lake that has been drying out in East London.
explanation.walkthrough: East London is a city in South Africa, and 'there' points to it; the answer is South African.
explanation.definitionFit: Vlei is a South African word for a low-lying marshy hollow or shallow seasonal lake.

clue.text: Lay fellows surrounding bishop must separate 15

indicators.note: separate means split apart, so the fellows word with bishop goes into the middle of the lay word

parts.note: to lay a bet is to wager

indicators.note: surrounding means placed round, so the fellows word is put about the bishop letter

parts.note: men are fellows
B is the chess notation abbreviation for bishop

explanation.surface: Non-clergy men gather around a bishop and must part company with another clue.
explanation.walkthrough: MEN 'surrounding' B gives MBEN, which 'must separate' WAGER into WA and GER. Lay looks like 'not clergy', which suits the bishop, but it is the verb to bet.
explanation.definitionFit: The wambenger is an Australian name for a phascogale, a small carnivorous marsupial.

clue.text: Bloomers as clothing for exercise, tucking in nearly half at the bottom before cycling

indicators.note: tucking in means taking something inside, so the clothing part goes back within the exercise part
the bottom four of the phrase's ten letters, nearly half of it, are the part that gets lifted and tucked in

parts.note: sports are activities done for exercise; with the next word they make sportswear, clothing for exercise

indicators.note: cycling means turning round in a loop, so the first of those lifted letters moves to their end before they go back in

parts.note: wear means clothing, as in 'evening wear'

explanation.surface: Women's knickers as gym kit, tucked in with almost half showing at the bottom.
explanation.walkthrough: Clothing for exercise is sportswear; its bottom near-half is the clothing word, which 'before cycling' loops its first letter to the end and 'tucking in' places after the first two letters. 'Bloomers' looks like underwear but means flowering plants.
explanation.definitionFit: Spearworts are buttercups with spear-shaped leaves; any flowering plant can be called a bloomer.

clue.text: Australian native holds tooth with light-coloured coating

indicators.note: a coating wraps round the outside of what it covers

parts.note: pale means light in colour
to hold something is to have it
a cog is a tooth on a gear wheel

explanation.surface: An Australian creature has a tooth with a pale film on it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Holds' looks like a container signal but simply gives a word meaning possesses.
explanation.definitionFit: The phascogale is a small carnivorous marsupial found only in Australia, so it is a native species there.

clue.text: Unusual sight of mountain pass to view within England's borders

parts.note: a gap is a pass between mountains

indicators.note: something within another word sits inside it
the borders of a word are its first and last letters

parts.note: the outer letters of England
to view is to see

explanation.surface: A traveller remarks on the rare sight from an English mountain pass.
explanation.definitionFit: Gapeseed is a dialect word for anything that makes people stare open-mouthed, a curiosity or spectacle.

clue.text: 13 regularly visited Touraine

indicators.note: visiting regularly means calling at every other spot, so alternate letters are kept

parts.note: first, third, fifth and seventh letters

explanation.surface: The creature at 13 has made regular trips to the Loire region of France.
explanation.definitionFit: Tuan is another Australian name for the phascogale, the same small marsupial clued at 13.

clue.text: Retreat into rehabilitation group with employer dismissing second former Chancellor

indicators.note: into means going inside, so the retreat word is placed within the rehab group's letters

parts.note: AA is Alcoholics Anonymous, a recovery group
a den is a private retreat

indicators.note: dismissing means sending away, so the letter for second is removed from the employer word

parts.note: a user is one who employs something

explanation.surface: A recovering addict withdraws into treatment while the boss sacks a deputy.
explanation.walkthrough: DEN goes 'into' AA for ADENA; USER 'dismissing' S leaves UER. Chancellor here is the German head of government, not a finance minister.
explanation.definitionFit: Konrad Adenauer was the first Chancellor of West Germany, from 1949 to 1963.

clue.text: "Horrible year" for a number in Elizabeth's reign?

indicators.note: something horrible is messed up, so the letters are jumbled

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Quoting the late Queen's 'annus horribilis' as one year among many in her reign.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface recalls Elizabeth II's 1992 'horrible year'; the definition means Elizabeth I's time, when a song was an ayre.
explanation.definitionFit: Ayre is the old spelling of air, a tune or song, typical of Elizabethan lute music, so a musical number.

clue.text: Punch mate, losing head over plugging angry companion, heavily once

indicators.note: plugging means filling a hole, so the shortened reversed mate goes inside the angry and companion letters

parts.note: upset means angry
CH is Companion of Honour, a British order

indicators.note: over means turned over, so the letters are read backwards
losing head means the first letter is dropped

parts.note: Judy is Punch's wife in the Punch and Judy puppet show

explanation.surface: A puppet hits his partner after an angry friend gets in the way.
explanation.walkthrough: Punch is the puppet, not a blow: in Punch and Judy his wife is Judy. 'losing head' and 'over' work on her name before it goes 'plugging' the other two pieces, between the E and T.
explanation.definitionFit: Upsey Dutch is an archaic phrase meaning in the Dutch manner, that is heavily or deeply, as in drinking.

clue.text: Trapped by hurricane, Azoreans brought up condition of hooter

indicators.note: brought up in a down entry means read from the bottom upward
letters trapped by other words are held inside them

parts.note: the end of hurricane and the start of Azoreans

explanation.surface: Islanders stuck in a storm come down with something nasty.
explanation.walkthrough: A hooter is slang for the nose.
explanation.definitionFit: Ozaena is a disease of the nose with a foul-smelling discharge, so a nasal condition.

clue.text: Master remains one holding a king's short sword

parts.note: start of WIZ, a whiz or expert

indicators.note: something holding other letters keeps them inside it

parts.note: ash is what remains after burning
K is king in chess and cards
rest of WIZ
taken as written
Roman numeral one

explanation.surface: A sword master stays on guard, holding the king's short blade.
explanation.walkthrough: W(A K)IZ then ASH and I.
explanation.definitionFit: The wakizashi is the shorter of the two swords traditionally carried by a samurai.

clue.text: Small hotel incorporates good, ace ingredient in bridie

indicators.note: one word incorporating others takes them into its body

parts.note: an inn is a small hotel
G for good
A for ace, as on playing cards

explanation.surface: A little hotel boasts a fine, first-rate filling in its bridies.
explanation.walkthrough: IN(GA)N. A bridie is a Scottish meat pasty, so a Scots word is wanted.
explanation.definitionFit: Ingan is the Scots word for onion, a standard filling alongside the minced meat in a Forfar bridie.

clue.text: Aged duke mostly having ruled lines going back

indicators.note: going back means travelling in reverse, so the letters are read from end to start
mostly means not all, so the last letter is dropped

parts.note: feint is the term for faint ruled lines on writing paper

explanation.surface: An elderly nobleman has mostly ruled lines that are retreating.
explanation.walkthrough: Duke is slang for a fist (put up your dukes), and aged marks the word as archaic. FEINT 'mostly' gives FEIN, read 'going back'.
explanation.definitionFit: Nief, or neif, is an archaic and dialect word for the fist, which is slang called a duke.

clue.text: Hot season in Paris stifles a picnic for old poets

indicators.note: to stifle something is to smother it by closing round it

parts.note: été is French for summer
H for hot, as on taps

explanation.surface: A French summer heatwave spoils a picnic.
explanation.walkthrough: A picnic means something easy; 'for old poets' marks the word as archaic poetic.
explanation.definitionFit: Ethe is an archaic word for easy, and an easy task is called a picnic, so poets once used it so.

clue.text: Note containing attention-seeking word is source of new information

indicators.note: a word containing another holds it inside

parts.note: re is a note of the sol-fa scale
hem, like ahem, is a cough to get attention

explanation.surface: A memo with a throat-clearing word in it turns out to be where the news comes from.
explanation.definitionFit: In linguistics the rheme is the part of a sentence that conveys new information about the topic.

clue.text: Perhaps aid group with word of doubt during awkward teen infatuation

indicators.note: something during another happens within it, so it is placed inside
awkward suggests clumsy disorder, so the letters are jumbled

parts.note: um is a hesitant word
taken as written
an NGO, a non-governmental organisation, is perhaps an aid group

explanation.surface: A charity worker has doubts about an awkward teenager's behaviour.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Perhaps' signals that the aid group is just one example of a broader class of organisation.
explanation.definitionFit: Engouement, borrowed from French, means an excessive fondness or craze, an infatuation.

clue.text: Assume tree is in parade

indicators.note: one thing being in another means it sits inside

parts.note: say, as in 'say it rains', means assume
the ash is a tree

explanation.surface: A spectator supposes there is a tree in the procession.
explanation.definitionFit: To sashay is to walk in a swaggering, showy way, much as to parade means to strut and show off.

clue.text: Hill-dweller went higher across river, facing upward

parts.note: an ant lives in an anthill

indicators.note: a word stretched across another spans it, enclosing it

parts.note: rose is past tense of rise
R for river on maps

explanation.surface: A hill creature climbs higher, over a river, and looks up.
explanation.walkthrough: ANT then RO(R)SE.
explanation.definitionFit: Antrorse is a botanical term for hairs or parts pointing forward or upward, toward the tip.
